summary_paragraph: A 60-year-old male with a history of kidney transplantation, heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, atrial fibrillation, and coronary artery disease was admitted for progressive dyspnea, fatigue, and abdominal distention. Evaluation revealed acute on chronic diastolic heart failure with volume overload, confirmed by elevated BNP and imaging. He was treated with intravenous furosemide and transitioned to a split dose of oral torsemide. Echocardiography showed preserved ejection fraction but a small to moderate pericardial effusion without tamponade, likely related to his heart failure exacerbation or a mild viral process. A Type 2 myocardial infarction was diagnosed based on mild troponin elevation and EKG changes, attributed to demand ischemia. His apixaban dose was reduced to 2.5 mg twice daily due to reduced kidney function, and transplant medications were continued unchanged. He improved clinically, was euvolemic at discharge, and was sent home with close follow-up in cardiology and transplant nephrology, including a repeat echocardiogram to monitor pericardial effusion.
problems: Acute on chronic diastolic (congestive) heart failure
Type 2 diabetes mellitus with diabetic chronic kidney disease
Hypertensive heart and chronic kidney disease with heart failure and stage 1 through stage 4 chronic kidney disease, or unspecified chronic kidney disease
